description: We are Stack Underflow: six people across Cancún, and Vietnam turning NASA data (TEMPO, POWER, GIBS) into a way of listening to the Earth: shifts in air, temperature, patterns we would otherwise miss. We believe protecting life starts with looking in time. More than a 48-hour challenge, we build to push what we thought possible, because exploring space is also a way of caring for Earth.
summary: SpotiEarth turns NASA Earth-science timelapses into music, so anyone can hear how the planet changes, including people who cannot see the images. We built a computer-vision engine (NumPy and OpenCV) that reads every frame of NASA GIBS and SVS visualizations, converts each pixel’s color into the physical value it represents, and summarizes it into features: how much, where, how many storms or hotspots, and how much it changed. In the browser, those features become sound: pitch follows the data, intensity drives volume and texture, and stereo position follows where the signal sits on the map. Each of our 15 datasets (rainfall, sea temperature, air quality, lightning, CO₂, ocean currents, vegetation and more) has its own instrument palette and is grouped into playlists. Users can sweep a sound radar across the map, hear the country or ocean under the cursor, navigate entirely by keyboard with a built-in voice guide, or stand inside a 360° globe that follows the phone’s gyroscope. Satellite data is usually visual only; SpotiEarth makes it something everyone can listen to, explore and understand.
details:
What it does and how it works

SpotiEarth turns NASA Earth-science visualizations into sound, so their changes can be heard as well as seen. Starting from the NASA Earth Information Center catalog provided by the challenge, we selected 15 visualizations and turned them into 15 tracks (428 frames) grouped into 6 playlists: air quality, weather, water, climate, oceans and agriculture.

3 come from NASA GIBS satellite layers: IMERG precipitation (2025), GHRSST sea surface temperature anomalies (one frame per August, 2003–2026) and MODIS NDVI vegetation (2024).

12 come from NASA SVS: GEOS-FP model forecasts (air temperature, wind, precipitation, humidity) and GEOS-CF model estimates (PM2.5, ozone, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides) covering about two weeks of October–November 2026, plus ECCO2 surface currents, the volumetric CO₂ globe (2021), lightning seen from the ISS (2017–2023) and Perpetual Ocean 2 (temperature). Three of them were extracted from SVS videos with OpenCV.

It works in three steps:

Measure (offline, Python). Our engine converts each pixel’s color back into the value it represents using the visualization’s color table: exact matches first, then the nearest color in CIELAB within a tolerance for compressed video frames. For the 3 GIBS layers we use NASA’s official color tables. SVS pages only publish an image of their color bar, so we rebuilt 10 tables from those images; some scales required documented assumptions, so those values are approximate. The CO₂ and lightning globes have no color bar, so for them we built a relative 0–1 brightness index, not physical units. Each frame is then summarized into area-weighted measurements: coverage, mean, 95th percentile, the share of the map above dataset-specific thresholds (for example, the WHO PM2.5 guideline of 15 µg/m³), the data’s center of mass, a 24 × 48 grid, and the same values for continents and ocean basins. No neural networks are used, only NumPy and OpenCV, so every number can be traced back to a pixel and a color table.

Store and serve. Command-line tools save each track in PostgreSQL (JSONB). A FastAPI service exposes three read-only endpoints under /api/v1, rate-limited to 60 requests per minute.

Sonify (in the browser). The site generates the sound live with the Web Audio API, 4 seconds per frame. Each dataset decides which measurement drives the melody, on a two-octave pentatonic scale: the average value in 8 tracks, the latitude of the data’s center in 5 (higher note = farther north), the polluted area for nitrogen oxides, and the share of the globe with flashes for lightning. Other measurements control volume and texture density, accent bells, the brightness of the timbre, and the stereo position (the longitude of the data’s center). Five tracks (humidity, two rainfall tracks, air temperature and vegetation) use synthesized nature sounds, where the land/ocean balance mixes a low rumble with waves. The other ten replace them with instrument textures: wine glasses that beat more as ozone rises, a woodblock pulse that speeds up with nitrogen oxides, a glockenspiel or saxello when the sea is cooler or warmer than normal. Melodies use 100 recorded samples from the public-domain VCSL library. Listeners can choose between four presets and three layer modes (nature, music or both).

Two examples from the real data: in the sea temperature track, the average anomaly goes from about 0.0 °C in 2003 to about 0.6 °C in 2023–2026, so the melody climbs over the years. In the 2025 rainfall track, the rain’s center moves to about 10° S in March and about 10° N in September, so the melody follows the seasonal shift of the tropical rain belt.

Ways to explore

Keyboard player: play, step through frames, and press D to hear the current frame described (key values and the region where they are highest).

Map click: plays a note pitched by the value at that point, and the voice names the country and continent, or the ocean.

Explore radar (E): a radar spins around the pointer and plays the data level it passes over, with four sounds from calm to intense based on the dataset’s thresholds.

Voice guide: off by default. It announces pages and reads buttons and sections when moving with Tab; the music lowers while the voice speaks.

360° globe: for the 12 flat-map tracks, the frames wrap around you inside a sphere. Look around by dragging, with the keyboard or with the phone’s gyroscope.

Benefits and intended impact

Earth-science visualizations are made to be seen. SpotiEarth offers another way in: listening. We built it so that blind and low-vision people, and anyone who prefers to listen, can follow the same NASA data: where it rains, how clean the air is, how the ocean is warming. We see it as a tool for classrooms, museums and science outreach.

Tools and technologies

Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic Settings, SQLAlchemy 2.0, PostgreSQL 18 (JSONB), SlowAPI.

Image processing: NumPy and OpenCV.

Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, three.js (with a custom crossfade shader), d3-geo, TopoJSON with Natural Earth borders (world-atlas), Lucide icons.

Browser APIs: Web Audio, Web Speech (the browser’s own voice, with no keys or external servers), and device orientation for the gyroscope.

Sound: 100 VCSL samples (CC0), about 4 MB, served from our own site.

Infrastructure and quality: Docker, Docker Compose, VS Code Dev Container, 48 unit tests with Python unittest, ESLint, pnpm.

SI tools: Claude (Claude Code) and Cursor for coding, debugging and documentation.

Hardware: none; it runs in a modern browser on a computer or phone.

Creativity

Each track combines several measurements at once (how much, where, how intense) into layered sound, and every dataset has its own palette chosen to match what it represents: a dark didgeridoo drone for smoke, a mechanical pulse for traffic and industry pollution, raindrops for rain. Beyond listening along a timeline, you can explore the data in space: clicking the map, sweeping the radar, or standing inside the 360° globe.

Factors we considered

Traceability: every value comes from a color table, each track credits its exact NASA source, and approximate scales and relative indices are documented in the code.

Honest data: GEOS fields are model forecasts and estimates, not satellite photos, and the playlists say so. Averages are weighted by real pixel area so the poles don’t count too much. We left out two Perpetual Ocean versions (salinity and depth) because their colors could not be read reliably as a single variable.

Accessibility: full keyboard control, a voice guide that is off by default to avoid two voices for screen-reader users, live regions that announce place names, and a 360° globe that skips its crossfade when the system asks for reduced motion.

Performance: heavy processing runs offline and the API only reads. The globe keeps only the current frame and the next three in memory. If a sample fails to load, the sound falls back to synthesis.

Browser limits: audio starts on the first interaction, and the gyroscope needs HTTPS and permission on iPhone.

Privacy: no accounts, API keys, analytics or tracking; preferences are saved only in the browser.

Limitations

Values read from SVS color bars are approximate, CO₂ and lightning are relative indices, the GEOS tracks cover only about two weeks, and the 360° globe works only with flat maps.
